claim: As many as 90% of all human cancers originate from epithelial tissues.
source: As many as 90% of all human cancers originate from epithelial tissues.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cancer origins.

claim: Epithelial cells physically attach to ECM via integrins.
source: Cells physically attach to ECM via integrins, a class of signaling molecules that serve to stimulate the survival and proliferation of cells in a matrix attachment-dependent manner (Hynes, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hynes, 2002.

claim: Loss of contact with proper ECM molecules results in initiation of anoikis.
source: Conversely, loss of contact with the proper ECM molecules results in initiation of a cell death program known as anoikis (Frisch and Screaton, 2001), and other constraints on cellular expansion.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Frisch and Screaton, 2001.

claim: Early stages of epithelial cancer progression are characterized by genetic changes that confer ability to survive and proliferate in the absence of appropriate matrix anchorage.
source: Early stages of epithelial cancer progression are universally characterized with genetic changes that confer ability to survive and proliferate in the absence of an appropriate matrix anchorage, which allows cellular expansion in a geometrically unconstrained manner.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about cancer progression.

claim: Tumor-derived subclones with greater metastatic capacity in vivo display increased self-aggregation in vitro.
source: Thus, tumor-derived subclones with greater metastatic capacity in vivo display increased self-aggregation in vitro; at the same time, subclones selected for increased in vitro aggregation were found to be more metastatic in mice (Updyke and Nicolson, 1986; Saiki et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Updyke and Nicolson, 1986 and Saiki et al., 1991.

claim: Subclones selected for increased in vitro aggregation were found to be more metastatic in mice.
source: Thus, tumor-derived subclones with greater metastatic capacity in vivo display increased self-aggregation in vitro; at the same time, subclones selected for increased in vitro aggregation were found to be more metastatic in mice (Updyke and Nicolson, 1986; Saiki et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Updyke and Nicolson, 1986 and Saiki et al., 1991.

claim: Clusters of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) have been identified from blood samples of breast, colorectal, prostate, and lung cancer patients.
source: Clusters of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) have been identified from the blood samples of breast, colorectal, prostate, and lung cancer patients as well as from mouse tumor models (Molnar et al., 2001; Stott et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Molnar et al., 2001; Stott et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2011.

claim: On average, 50% of all breast and lung CTCs exist in circulation as aggregates.
source: In particular, one report demonstrated that, on average, 50% of all breast and lung CTCs exist in circulation as aggregates (Cho et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2012.

claim: Heterotypic interactions of cancer cells with the endothelial lining within the target organ microvasculature were documented as an initiating event for metastatic lesion formation.
source: Thus, heterotypic interactions of cancer cells with the endothelial lining within the target organ microvasculature were documented as an initiating event for metastatic lesion formation (Al-Mehdi et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Al-Mehdi et al., 2000.

claim: Signaling elicited by physical association of cancer cells with platelets and macrophages has been demonstrated to be essential for successful seeding and metastatic outgrowth.
source: Moreover, signaling elicited by the physical association of cancer cells with other cell types, such as platelets and macrophages, has been demonstrated to be essential for successful seeding and metastatic outgrowth (Chen et al., 2011; Labelle et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2011 and Labelle et al., 2011.

claim: A genetic screen identified PVRL4 as a potent mediator of anchorage-independent colony formation.
source: Our screen identified a cell adhesion molecule PVRL4 (poliovirus receptor-like 4), also known as Nectin-4, which we demonstrate to be a potent mediator of anchorage-independent colony formation in normal epithelial and cancer cells alike.
evidence: This claim is based on the results of the genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: PVRL4 promotes attachment of individual cells to each other via engaging its receptor PVRL1 on a juxtaposed cell.
source: We demonstrate that PVRL4 promotes the attachment of individual cells to each other via engaging its receptor PVRL1 on a juxtaposed cell.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PVRL4-mediated cell-to-cell attachment triggers integrin β4 signaling in a matrix attachment-independent manner.
source: PVRL4-mediated cell-to-cell attachment triggers integrin β4 signaling in a matrix attachment-independent manner, and interfering with this pathway blocks PVRL4-driven anchorage-independence.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Blocking PVRL4-driven cell–cell contact assembly with monoclonal antibodies potently inhibits anchorage-independent cellular expansion in vitro.
source: Finally, we show that blocking PVRL4-driven cell–cell contact assembly with monoclonal antibodies potently inhibits anchorage-independent cellular expansion in vitro as well as the growth of orthotopically implanted tumors in vivo, thus validating the therapeutic utility of this approach.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Blocking PVRL4-driven cell–cell contact assembly with monoclonal antibodies inhibits the growth of orthotopically implanted tumors in vivo.
source: Finally, we show that blocking PVRL4-driven cell–cell contact assembly with monoclonal antibodies potently inhibits anchorage-independent cellular expansion in vitro as well as the growth of orthotopically implanted tumors in vivo, thus validating the therapeutic utility of this approach.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TL-HMECs cannot survive and proliferate in semi-solid medium in the absence of substratum attachment.
source: TL-HMECs cannot survive and proliferate in a semi-solid medium, such as methylcellulose, in the absence of substratum attachment; however, ectopic expression of oncogenic H-RASV12, myristoylated PI3K catalytic subunit (Zhao et al., 2003), or shRNA against PTEN (Westbrook et al., 2005) enables anchorage-independent cellular expansion and formation of macroscopic colonies.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental model used in the study.

claim: Ectopic expression of oncogenic H-RASV12 enables anchorage-independent cellular expansion and formation of macroscopic colonies in TL-HMECs.
source: TL-HMECs cannot survive and proliferate in a semi-solid medium, such as methylcellulose, in the absence of substratum attachment; however, ectopic expression of oncogenic H-RASV12, myristoylated PI3K catalytic subunit (Zhao et al., 2003), or shRNA against PTEN (Westbrook et al., 2005) enables anchorage-independent cellular expansion and formation of macroscopic colonies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: Ectopic expression of myristoylated PI3K catalytic subunit enables anchorage-independent cellular expansion and formation of macroscopic colonies in TL-HMECs.
source: TL-HMECs cannot survive and proliferate in a semi-solid medium, such as methylcellulose, in the absence of substratum attachment; however, ectopic expression of oncogenic H-RASV12, myristoylated PI3K catalytic subunit (Zhao et al., 2003), or shRNA against PTEN (Westbrook et al., 2005) enables anchorage-independent cellular expansion and formation of macroscopic colonies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Zhao et al., 2003.

claim: shRNA against PTEN enables anchorage-independent cellular expansion and formation of macroscopic colonies in TL-HMECs.
source: TL-HMECs cannot survive and proliferate in a semi-solid medium, such as methylcellulose, in the absence of substratum attachment; however, ectopic expression of oncogenic H-RASV12, myristoylated PI3K catalytic subunit (Zhao et al., 2003), or shRNA against PTEN (Westbrook et al., 2005) enables anchorage-independent cellular expansion and formation of macroscopic colonies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Westbrook et al., 2005.

claim: Eight out of 11 ORFs that potently induced anchorage-independent growth localized to statistically defined peaks of focal amplification in at least one tumor subtype.
source: According to the recently published copy number variation analysis across a variety of tumor types (Beroukhim et al., 2010), eight out of 11 ORFs that potently induced anchorage-independent growth localized to statistically defined peaks of focal amplification in at least one tumor subtype (p=0.009, Fisher's exact test), providing strong evidence for positive selection of these genes in cancer (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of copy number variation data from Beroukhim et al., 2010.

claim: Ectopic expression of SULF2 had been previously found to induce anchorage-independent growth in human bronchial epithelial cells.
source: Ectopic expression of SULF2 (sulfatase 2) had been previously found to induce anchorage-independent growth in human bronchial epithelial cells (Lemjabbar-Alaoui et al., 2010) and NPM1 (nucleophosmin 1) overexpression had been previously found to enable NIH 3T3 fibroblast colony formation in methylcellulose (Kondo et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lemjabbar-Alaoui et al., 2010.

claim: NPM1 overexpression had been previously found to enable NIH 3T3 fibroblast colony formation in methylcellulose.
source: Ectopic expression of SULF2 (sulfatase 2) had been previously found to induce anchorage-independent growth in human bronchial epithelial cells (Lemjabbar-Alaoui et al., 2010) and NPM1 (nucleophosmin 1) overexpression had been previously found to enable NIH 3T3 fibroblast colony formation in methylcellulose (Kondo et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kondo et al., 1997.

claim: Endogenous expression of PVRL4 was not detectable in TL-HMECs.
source: Ectopic expression of PVRL4 strongly induced anchorage-independent colony formation (Figure 1B), whereas its endogenous expression was not detectable in TL-HMECs (Figure 2B), consistent with the documented absence of its expression in normal mammary gland (Fabre-Lafay et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B and supported by a citation to Fabre-Lafay et al., 2007.

claim: PVRL4 expression is absent in normal mammary gland.
source: Ectopic expression of PVRL4 strongly induced anchorage-independent colony formation (Figure 1B), whereas its endogenous expression was not detectable in TL-HMECs (Figure 2B), consistent with the documented absence of its expression in normal mammary gland (Fabre-Lafay et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fabre-Lafay et al., 2007.

claim: PVRL4 belongs to a family of poliovirus receptor-related transmembrane proteins, also known as nectins.
source: Recently identified to be a receptor for measles virus, PVRL4 (Muhlebach et al., 2011; Noyce et al., 2011) belongs to a family of poliovirus receptor-related transmembrane proteins, also known as nectins, which localize to sites of cell junctions in various cell types (reviewed in Takai et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Muhlebach et al., 2011; Noyce et al., 2011; and Takai et al., 2008.

claim: PVRL4 contains an extracellular region with three immunoglobulin-like domains, a single transmembrane domain, and a short cytoplasmic tail.
source: Similarly to other nectins, PVRL4 contains an extracellular region with three immunoglobulin-like domains, a single transmembrane domain, and a short cytoplasmic tail (Reymond et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reymond et al., 2001.

claim: Deletion of the entire cytoplasmic region of PVRL4 did not affect its ability to promote TL-HMEC colony formation.
source: Remarkably, deletion of the entire cytoplasmic region of PVRL4 did not affect its ability to promote TL-HMEC colony formation (Figure 2C) or cell viability (Figure 2D) in the absence of substratum attachment.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of the entire cytoplasmic region of PVRL4 did not affect cell viability in the absence of substratum attachment.
source: Remarkably, deletion of the entire cytoplasmic region of PVRL4 did not affect its ability to promote TL-HMEC colony formation (Figure 2C) or cell viability (Figure 2D) in the absence of substratum attachment.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both full-length PVRL4 and its cytoplasmic deletion mutant reduced upregulation of squamous differentiation markers in TL-HMECs cultured in suspension.
source: TL-HMECs in particular do not initiate classic apoptotic responses in response to the loss of substratum attachment, likely due to the anti-apoptotic action of Large T antigen (not shown), but instead potently upregulate multiple squamous differentiation markers, including TGM1 (transglutaminase 1), KRT6A (keratin 6), and IVL (involucrin), and we found that both full-length PVRL4 and its cytoplasmic deletion mutant reduced this effect (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: PVRL4 protects TL-HMECs from differentiation associated with anchorage loss.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that PVRL4 protects TL-HMECs from the differentiation associated with anchorage loss and promotes subsequent cellular expansion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The anchorage-independence phenotype is facilitated by the extracellular part of PVRL4 rather than by its intracellular region.
source: Importantly, this phenotype is facilitated by the extracellular part of PVRL4 rather than by its intracellular region.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the deletion mutant experiments.

claim: PVRL4 drives rapid association of TL-HMECs into multicellular clusters in suspension.
source: Consistent with its role in promoting cell–cell contact formation, PVRL4 drives rapid association of TL-HMECs into multicellular clusters in suspension (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Out of 56 colonies from PVRL4-expressing cells seeded immediately into methylcellulose, all 56 were single-color colonies.
source: Examining the colors of resulting colonies revealed that out of 56 colonies from sample (i), all 56 were single-color colonies, whereas in sample (ii), 39 out of 40 colonies were single-color, and only one colony contained both GFP and dsRed-positive cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Passing cells through a 35 μm cell strainer immediately prior to being seeded in the absence of anchorage did not affect colony numbers.
source: Consistent with this observation, passing cells through a 35 μm cell strainer immediately prior to being seeded in the absence of anchorage did not affect colony numbers (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), further confirming that PVRL4-induced colonies are clonal in origin and that the observed increase in colony numbers is not a result of pre-existing multicellular clusters having a survival advantage over single cells in the absence of anchorage.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The extracellular region of PVRL4 exhibits preferential affinity for trans-interaction with PVRL1.
source: The extracellular region of PVRL4 exhibits preferential affinity for trans-interaction with PVRL1 (Reymond et al., 2001), a cell adhesion molecule endogenously expressed in TL-HMECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reymond et al., 2001.

claim: PVRL1 depletion resulted in exclusion of dsRed-labeled cells from multicellular clusters formed by PVRL4-expressing GFP-labeled TL-HMECs.
source: PVRL1 depletion resulted in exclusion of dsRed-labeled cells from multicellular clusters, whereas control shRNA-expressing cells were readily incorporated (Figure 3C), suggesting that PVRL4-mediated cell–cell contacts are carried out through interaction with its receptor PVRL1.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Stable depletion of the PVRL1 transcript by two independent shRNA constructs abolished anchorage-independent colony formation induced by PVRL4.
source: Indeed, stable depletion of the PVRL1 transcript by two independent shRNA constructs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) abolished anchorage-independent colony formation (Figure 3D), paralleling the effect of PVRL1 depletion on PVRL4-driven cell-to-cell attachment.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cell clustering was completely abrogated in the presence of three independent PVRL4 antibodies.
source: Cell clustering was completely abrogated in the presence of three independent PVRL4 antibodies, whereas control IgG or a blocking antibody against E-cadherin (DECMA-1) did not produce such an effect (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: An antibody targeting the extracellular region of PVRL1 inhibited PVRL4-induced cell clustering.
source: Similarly, an antibody targeting the extracellular region of PVRL1 inhibited PVRL4-induced cell clustering (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: PVRL4-driven colony formation was inhibited to almost a basal level in the presence of a monoclonal antibody targeting the extracellular region of PVRL4.
source: PVRL4-driven colony formation was inhibited to almost a basal level in the presence of a monoclonal antibody targeting the extracellular region of PVRL4, but no such effect was observed on colonies induced by PTEN shRNA (Figure 3F), demonstrating that the observed inhibition is due to a direct effect of an antibody and not due to its general toxicity.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Expression of PVRL4-CD8tm induced both cell clustering and anchorage-independent colony formation.
source: Expression of PVRL4-CD8tm induced both cell clustering and anchorage-independent colony formation, and both phenotypes were suppressed by stable depletion of endogenous PVRL1 (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Both cell clustering and colony formation defects induced by PVRL1 shRNA were rescued by the expression of the shRNA-resistant PVRL1-CD8tm construct.
source: Both cell clustering and colony formation defects induced by PVRL1 shRNA were rescued by the expression of the shRNA-resistant PVRL1-CD8tm construct.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ability to withstand the absence of anchorage is driven by the PVRL4-PVRL1 cell-surface trans-interaction and not by intracellular or transmembrane regions of either molecule.
source: Taken together, these data indicate an on-target nature of the PVRL1 depletion phenotype and demonstrate that ability to withstand the absence of anchorage is driven by the PVRL4-PVRL1 cell-surface trans-interaction and not by intracellular or transmembrane regions of either molecule.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chimeric construct experiments.

claim: Expression of mutant RasV12 triggered multicellular cluster formation in TL-HMECs.
source: Either expression of mutant RasV12, or myristoylated PI3K catalytic subunit (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), or shRNA-mediated depletion of PTEN (Figure 4—figure supplement 5; for depletion efficiencies see Figure 4—figure supplement 6) triggered multicellular cluster formation in TL-HMECs.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Expression of myristoylated PI3K catalytic subunit triggered multicellular cluster formation in TL-HMECs.
source: Either expression of mutant RasV12, or myristoylated PI3K catalytic subunit (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), or shRNA-mediated depletion of PTEN (Figure 4—figure supplement 5; for depletion efficiencies see Figure 4—figure supplement 6) triggered multicellular cluster formation in TL-HMECs.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: shRNA-mediated depletion of PTEN triggered multicellular cluster formation in TL-HMECs.
source: Either expression of mutant RasV12, or myristoylated PI3K catalytic subunit (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), or shRNA-mediated depletion of PTEN (Figure 4—figure supplement 5; for depletion efficiencies see Figure 4—figure supplement 6) triggered multicellular cluster formation in TL-HMECs.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: Integrin β4 was identified as specifically interacting with HA/FLAG-PVRL4 by mass spectrometry.
source: We identified the transmembrane protein integrin β4 as specifically interacting with HA/FLAG-PVRL4 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Immunoblotting verified a specific association of integrin β4 with PVRL4 in suspension-incubated TL-HMECs.
source: To validate the putative PVRL4–integrin β4 interaction directly in cells under conditions of anchorage deprivation, we performed immunoprecipitations with anti-HA beads from lysates of suspension-incubated TL-HMECs that expressed either HA/FLAG-tagged PVRL4 or HA/FLAG-tagged GFP. Immunoblotting for integrin β4 verified a specific association of integrin β4 with PVRL4 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The same amount of integrin β4 coprecipitated with HA/FLAG-tagged PVRL4 from lysates prepared from multicellular clusters and from single-cell suspension.
source: The same amount of integrin β4 coprecipitated with HA/FLAG-tagged PVRL4 from lysates prepared from multicellular clusters and from single-cell suspension.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The amount of coprecipitating integrin β4 was not affected by RNAi-mediated depletion of PVRL1.
source: Similarly, the amount of coprecipitating integrin β4 was not affected by RNAi-mediated depletion of PVRL1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both full-length and cytoplasmic deletion version of PVRL4 coprecipitated with integrin β4.
source: Immunoprecipitation of integrin β4 from TL-HMECs which were induced to express either a full-length or a cytoplasmic deletion version of PVRL4 revealed that both full-length and mutant versions of PVRL4 coprecipitated with integrin β4, and not with a control IgG (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PVRL4-induced anchorage-independent colony formation was markedly reduced in the presence of integrin β4-specific shRNAs.
source: Depletion of integrin β4 had no effect on TL-HMEC attachment to the tissue culture vessel or on proliferation in adherent conditions; neither did it affect PVRL4-driven cell clustering (not shown). However, PVRL4-induced anchorage-independent colony formation was markedly reduced in the presence of integrin β4-specific shRNAs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PI3K-driven colony numbers were not affected by integrin β4 depletion.
source: Importantly, reliance on integrin β4 was specific to colony growth promoted by PVRL4, as PI3K-driven colony numbers were not affected by its depletion.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Levels of activated SFK dropped precipitously in control cells while remaining high in PVRL4-expressing cells after 6 hr incubation in suspension.
source: Levels of activated SFK dropped precipitously in control cells while remaining high in PVRL4-expressing cells but not in PVRL4-expressing, PVRL1-depleted cells.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The addition of anti-PVRL4 antibody reduced the level of SFK autophosphorylation in suspension.
source: Moreover, the addition of anti-PVRL4 antibody also reduced the level of SFK autophosphorylation in suspension.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Levels of SFK activation observed in freshly detached cells were maintained in cells that were allowed to attach to each other but not in cells in which clustering was prevented by either anti-PVRL4 antibody or PVRL1 depletion.
source: A similar effect was observed after a short-term incubation of PVRL4-expressing TL-HMECs in suspension (Figure 5F), where levels of SFK activation observed in freshly detached cells (0 hr time point) were maintained in cells that were allowed to attach to each other but not in cells in which clustering was prevented by either anti-PVRL4 antibody or PVRL1 depletion.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: PVRL4-driven but not PI3K-driven anchorage-independent colony formation was abrogated in the presence of PP2, a chemical inhibitor of SFK activity.
source: In support of this, PVRL4-driven but not PI3K-driven anchorage-independent colony formation was abrogated in the presence of PP2, a chemical inhibitor of SFK activity (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Two independent shRNAs against SHP-2 completely abrogated colony formation induced by PVRL4.
source: Indeed, two independent shRNAs against SHP-2 completely abrogated colony formation induced by PVRL4 (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 5H and 5I.

claim: SUM190 cells contain a high-level focal amplification of the PVRL4 genomic locus.
source: We first focused on an inflammatory breast tumor cell line SUM190, which contains a particularly high-level focal amplification (∼50 kb) of the PVRL4 genomic locus (Figure 6A) (Beroukhim et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on genomic data shown in Figure 6A and supported by a citation to Beroukhim et al., 2010.

claim: Spontaneous self-clustering of SUM190 cells was abrogated by anti-PVRL4 antibodies.
source: Paralleling effects seen in TL-HMECs, spontaneous self-clustering of SUM190 cells was abrogated by anti-PVRL4 antibodies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) or by RNAi against PVRL4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Heterotypic attachment of SUM190 cells with human lung microvascular endothelial (HMVEC-L) cells was prevented by anti-PVRL4 antibodies.
source: Similarly, heterotypic attachment of SUM190 cells with human lung microvascular endothelial (HMVEC-L) cells was prevented by anti-PVRL4 antibodies (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) and by RNAi (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: RNAi against PVRL4 potently reduced both anchorage-independent colony formation and clonogenic growth of SUM190 cells.
source: RNAi against PVRL4 potently reduced both anchorage-independent colony formation and clonogenic growth of SUM190 cells, indicating that PVRL4 is involved in the growth and survival of breast cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Expression of anti-PVRL4 shRNAs in Sk-BR-3 and BT-474 cells resulted in a strong defect in clonogenic growth.
source: To verify that the effects of PVRL4 depletion are not limited to SUM190 cells, we expressed anti-PVRL4 shRNAs in two additional breast cancer cell lines, Sk-BR-3 and BT-474 (Figure 6—figure supplement 5), which both express lower levels of PVRL4 than SUM190 cells (Fabre-Lafay et al., 2007), and observed a strong defect in clonogenic growth (Figure 6—figure supplement 6) and reduced proliferation in the absence of anchorage (Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6 and supported by a citation to Fabre-Lafay et al., 2007.

claim: Coexpression of PVRL4-CD8tm in the presence of PVRL4-targeting shRNAs alleviated the clonogenic survival defect in SUM190 cells.
source: Coexpression of PVRL4-CD8tm in the presence of PVRL4-targeting shRNAs alleviated the clonogenic survival defect, confirming its on-target nature (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: The extracellular region of PVRL4 alone is sufficient for potentiating clonogenic survival of breast cancer cells.
source: This result also demonstrates that the extracellular region of PVRL4 alone is sufficient for potentiating clonogenic survival of breast cancer cells, consistent with PVRL4-CD8tm ability to enable anchorage-independent colony formation in TL-HMECs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiment with PVRL4-CD8tm.

claim: Depletion of PVRL4 by RNAi from SUM190 cells inhibited xenograft growth.
source: Depletion of PVRL4 by RNAi from SUM190 (Figure 7A,B), SUM185 (Figure 7C), and BT-474 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) inhibited xenograft growth, verifying the importance of PVRL4 to cancer cell growth in vivo as well as in vitro.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 7A, 7B, and 7C.

claim: Depletion of PVRL4 by RNAi from SUM185 cells inhibited xenograft growth.
source: Depletion of PVRL4 by RNAi from SUM190 (Figure 7A,B), SUM185 (Figure 7C), and BT-474 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) inhibited xenograft growth, verifying the importance of PVRL4 to cancer cell growth in vivo as well as in vitro.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Depletion of PVRL4 by RNAi from BT-474 cells inhibited xenograft growth.
source: Depletion of PVRL4 by RNAi from SUM190 (Figure 7A,B), SUM185 (Figure 7C), and BT-474 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) inhibited xenograft growth, verifying the importance of PVRL4 to cancer cell growth in vivo as well as in vitro.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PVRL4 antibody-treated group displayed a remarkable stalling of tumor growth throughout the course of the injection regimen.
source: Whereas tumor volumes in the control group steadily increased over time, the PVRL4 antibody-treated group displayed a remarkable stalling of tumor growth throughout the course of the injection regimen (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: PVRL4 antibody treatment resulted in a precipitous decline of PVRL4 protein levels in tumor lysates.
source: Immunoblotting of tumor lysates revealed that PVRL4 antibody treatment resulted in a precipitous decline of PVRL4 protein levels, suggesting that cells with the highest expression of PVRL4 were eliminated by the treatment (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Histological analysis revealed areas of widespread necrosis and loss of cell contacts in anti-PVRL4 antibody-treated tumors compared to control IgG-treated tumors.
source: This latter observation was corroborated by histological analysis (Figure 7F), which revealed areas of widespread necrosis and, importantly, loss of cell contacts (Figure 7D–F) when compared to control IgG-treated tumors (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Examination of three-dimensional tumor architecture revealed reduced cell–cell contacts in anti-PVRL4 antibody-treated samples as compared to controls.
source: Finally, examination of three-dimensional tumor architecture in control- and anti-PVRL4 antibody-treated tumors by two-photon confocal microscopy revealed reduced cell–cell contacts in anti-PVRL4 antibody-treated samples as compared to controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: No increase in cell lysis was observed with anti-PVRL4 antibody over isotype control-incubated cells in an ADCC assay.
source: No increase in cell lysis was observed with anti-PVRL4 antibody over isotype control-incubated cells, demonstrating that anti-PVRL4 antibody was unable to efficiently recruit Fc receptor-containing cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining revealed no differences in the extent of macrophage infiltration between control and anti-PVRL4 IgG-treated tumor sections.
source: Moreover, immunohistochemical staining of control and anti-PVRL4 IgG-treated tumor sections for a mouse macrophage-specific marker F4/80 revealed no differences in the extent of macrophage infiltration (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: E-cadherin and vimentin protein levels remained unchanged in SUM190 xenografts treated with anti-PVRL4 antibody in vivo.
source: To address this, we measured levels of E-cadherin (an epithelial marker) and vimentin (a mesenchymal marker) in SUM190 xenografts treated with anti-PVRL4 antibody in vivo (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A) as well as in cultured SUM190 cells in which PVRL4 expression was inhibited by RNAi (Figure 7—figure supplement 5B). In both settings E-cadherin and vimentin protein levels remained unchanged, demonstrating that inhibiting PVRL4 in SUM190 cells does not cause EMT; neither does it select for cells with EMT-like characteristics in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5A.

claim: E-cadherin and vimentin protein levels remained unchanged in cultured SUM190 cells in which PVRL4 expression was inhibited by RNAi.
source: To address this, we measured levels of E-cadherin (an epithelial marker) and vimentin (a mesenchymal marker) in SUM190 xenografts treated with anti-PVRL4 antibody in vivo (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A) as well as in cultured SUM190 cells in which PVRL4 expression was inhibited by RNAi (Figure 7—figure supplement 5B). In both settings E-cadherin and vimentin protein levels remained unchanged, demonstrating that inhibiting PVRL4 in SUM190 cells does not cause EMT; neither does it select for cells with EMT-like characteristics in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Both human and mouse PVRL4 were strongly recognized by anti-PVRL4 antibody when expressed on the cell surface.
source: Both human and mouse PVRL4 were strongly recognized by anti-PVRL4 antibody when expressed on the cell surface (Figure 7—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6.

claim: The skin surface of mice treated with anti-PVRL4 antibodies was not visibly affected by treatment, and mice appeared healthy overall.
source: The skin surface of mice treated with anti-PVRL4 antibodies was not visibly affected by treatment, and mice appeared healthy overall, demonstrating that targeted therapy against PVRL4 does not induce acute side effects in this organism.
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo experiments.

claim: PVRL4 is expressed in a limited set of normal tissues—namely, skin epidermis, hair follicles, placenta, trachea, and lung.
source: PVRL4 is expressed in a limited set of normal tissues—namely, skin epidermis, hair follicles, placenta, trachea, and lung (Jelani et al., 2011)—yet it becomes overexpressed in a large fraction of breast (Fabre-Lafay et al., 2007), NSCLC (Takano et al., 2009), and ovarian (Derycke et al., 2010) tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jelani et al., 2011.

claim: PVRL4 becomes overexpressed in a large fraction of breast tumors.
source: PVRL4 is expressed in a limited set of normal tissues—namely, skin epidermis, hair follicles, placenta, trachea, and lung (Jelani et al., 2011)—yet it becomes overexpressed in a large fraction of breast (Fabre-Lafay et al., 2007), NSCLC (Takano et al., 2009), and ovarian (Derycke et al., 2010) tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fabre-Lafay et al., 2007.

claim: PVRL4 becomes overexpressed in a large fraction of NSCLC tumors.
source: PVRL4 is expressed in a limited set of normal tissues—namely, skin epidermis, hair follicles, placenta, trachea, and lung (Jelani et al., 2011)—yet it becomes overexpressed in a large fraction of breast (Fabre-Lafay et al., 2007), NSCLC (Takano et al., 2009), and ovarian (Derycke et al., 2010) tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takano et al., 2009.

claim: PVRL4 becomes overexpressed in a large fraction of ovarian tumors.
source: PVRL4 is expressed in a limited set of normal tissues—namely, skin epidermis, hair follicles, placenta, trachea, and lung (Jelani et al., 2011)—yet it becomes overexpressed in a large fraction of breast (Fabre-Lafay et al., 2007), NSCLC (Takano et al., 2009), and ovarian (Derycke et al., 2010) tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Derycke et al., 2010.

claim: Analysis of a publicly available dataset indicates a low-level copy number gain of PVRL4 in 60.3% of 484 breast tumor samples.
source: Analysis of a publicly available dataset of copy number alterations involving PVRL4 in 484 breast tumors indicates a low-level copy number gain in 60.3% of samples, and high-level amplification in another 7.9% of samples (Cerami et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of data from Cerami et al., 2012.

claim: Analysis of a publicly available dataset indicates high-level amplification of PVRL4 in 7.9% of 484 breast tumor samples.
source: Analysis of a publicly available dataset of copy number alterations involving PVRL4 in 484 breast tumors indicates a low-level copy number gain in 60.3% of samples, and high-level amplification in another 7.9% of samples (Cerami et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of data from Cerami et al., 2012.

claim: PVRL4 has emerged as a strong predictor of poor postoperative survival of patients with breast and lung cancer.
source: Moreover, PVRL4 has emerged as a strong predictor of poor postoperative survival of patients with breast and lung cancer (Takano et al., 2009; Athanassiadou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Takano et al., 2009 and Athanassiadou et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of afadin has been shown to be strongly associated with poor outcome in breast cancer patients.
source: Interestingly, and in contrast to PVRL4, loss of afadin has been shown to be strongly associated with poor outcome in breast cancer patients in a number of studies (Letessier et al., 2007; Fournier et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Letessier et al., 2007 and Fournier et al., 2011.

claim: In lung cancer cells, siRNA-mediated depletion of PVRL4 was shown to negatively affect adherent growth and motility.
source: In lung cancer cells, siRNA-mediated depletion of PVRL4 was shown to negatively affect adherent growth and motility (Takano et al., 2009), highlighting the functional role of PVRL4 across multiple cancer types.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takano et al., 2009.

claim: Integrin β4 expression is associated with poor prognosis and a basal-like expression profile.
source: Similarly to PVRL4, integrin β4 expression is associated with poor prognosis and a basal-like expression profile (Diaz et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2008), and targeting integrin β4 with RNAi was shown to inhibit anchorage-independent growth, invasion, and xenograft growth in breast cancer cell lines (Lipscomb et al., 2003; Bon et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Diaz et al., 2005 and Lu et al., 2008.

claim: Targeting integrin β4 with RNAi was shown to inhibit anchorage-independent growth, invasion, and xenograft growth in breast cancer cell lines.
source: Similarly to PVRL4, integrin β4 expression is associated with poor prognosis and a basal-like expression profile (Diaz et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2008), and targeting integrin β4 with RNAi was shown to inhibit anchorage-independent growth, invasion, and xenograft growth in breast cancer cell lines (Lipscomb et al., 2003; Bon et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lipscomb et al., 2003 and Bon et al., 2006.

claim: Dimerization of chimeric molecules containing the cytoplasmic region of integrin β4 on the cell surface by adding TrkB ligand was sufficient to drive SFK activation in a manner dependent on SHP-2 phosphatase.
source: This signaling autonomy was convincingly demonstrated in a study utilizing chimeric constructs where extracellular and transmembrane regions of integrin β4 were substituted with those on the TrkB receptor tyrosine kinase. Dimerization of two such chimeric molecules on the cell surface by adding TrkB ligand, BDNF, was sufficient to drive SFK activation, in a manner dependent on SHP-2 phosphatase (Merdek et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Merdek et al., 2007.

claim: Increased clustering has been previously associated with greater metastatic capacity.
source: Increased clustering has been previously associated with greater metastatic capacity (Updyke and Nicolson, 1986), raising an interesting possibility that increased cell–cell adhesiveness is a generalized mechanism that tumor cells employ as a part of their survival strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Updyke and Nicolson, 1986.

claim: 100% of breast tumors from patients with two or more lymph nodes that are positive for cancer cells express PVRL4.
source: This is particularly relevant for PVRL4 as 100% of breast tumors from patients with two or more lymph nodes that are positive for cancer cells express PVRL4 (Athanassiadou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Athanassiadou et al., 2011.
